queue.mechanics: The ingress module appends work before dispatch scans it.
queue.detail: A committed row is visible after restart; an in-memory notification is only a hint.

high.prompt: A task was accepted just before a restart. Why is a durable queue useful?
options: Reconstruct work from the worker count

medium.prompt: The process restarts. Where should pending work come from?

low.prompt: After process death, which artifact proves acceptance?
options: An entry in the in-memory dispatcher
A free slot in the worker pool

clock.mechanics: The scheduler compares its own clock with the stored claim deadline.
clock.detail: Eligibility begins at now ≥ deadline; a client clock cannot extend the boundary.

high.prompt: A worker stops reporting and still holds its claim. What can a deadline help the dispatcher do?

medium.prompt: A worker and scheduler disagree about the time. Whose clock decides whether the claim has expired?

low.prompt: At exactly the stored deadline, is the old claim eligible for replacement here?

lease.mechanics: The dispatcher grants a lease. After expiry it can grant a new one. The result writer must still distinguish the two owners.
lease.detail: A lease carries a monotonically increasing generation. Commit checks the active generation atomically; an expired worker cannot overwrite a newer attempt.

high.prompt: A worker disappears before reporting a result. What does letting its claim expire accomplish?
options: Keep the same worker assigned forever

medium.prompt: Worker A’s claim expires, then B takes over. Both finish. Which result may become durable?

low.prompt: A task is reassigned during a result write. Which predicate can safely guard the atomic write?
options: Task ID and worker start time
Task ID and time of arrival

fence.mechanics: The result writer matches the claim generation against the active lease before publishing output.
fence.detail: Commit and generation comparison share one transaction. A stale generation affects zero rows.

high.prompt: An old worker finishes after a new owner takes over. What protection does a write fence give?
options: Keep an old owner from replacing a newer result
Stop old workers from using CPU
Reduce the time spent executing the task
Make both workers’ results publish together

medium.prompt: A worker submits a result after its task was reassigned. Which comparison protects the write?

low.prompt: The guarded update touched zero rows. What should the old worker infer?
options: The write was merged into the new lease

journal.mechanics: The journal records accepted state transitions; the dashboard projects them into a timeline.
journal.detail: A stable event ID makes replay idempotent; the cursor advances only after application.

high.prompt: The dashboard restarts with an empty timeline. What can a saved journal help it do?
options: Discover which worker is currently using the most CPU
Retry every job from the beginning

medium.prompt: During replay, the same event appears twice. What matters?
options: Its position in the current response

low.prompt: An event was read but the application crashed while applying it. When can the replay cursor safely advance?
options: As soon as the event is read
After a replay process acquires a lock

recovery.mechanics: The recovery pass reloads queued tasks, checks leases and reconciles the journal.
recovery.detail: A live generation must not be displaced by a restart; only expired claims become eligible.

high.prompt: A dispatcher restarts while a task is still running. What should recovery preserve?
options: Only the most recent completed result

medium.prompt: After restart, which task is eligible for reassignment?
options: A task that already has a saved result

low.prompt: A recovery scan sees a live unexpired claim. What happens?
options: Bump its generation on every scan
Drop the task from the queue

retry.mechanics: The delivery loop schedules a bounded retry rather than immediately flooding the receiver.
retry.detail: Persist attempt number and next eligible time with the job.

high.prompt: A receiver has started returning temporary failures. What does delaying another attempt give it?
options: A second copy of every job

medium.prompt: A job has another attempt scheduled for later. When should the retry loop send it?
options: Once a new worker is hired

low.prompt: Which fields must survive a retry-loop restart?
options: Attempt count and next eligible time
Only the last worker’s log line

delivery.mechanics: The dispatcher measures a response and acknowledges successful deliveries.
delivery.detail: A durable acknowledgment suppresses replay of a confirmed job.

high.prompt: A completed result is ready to be sent to its receiver. What does the delivery loop connect?
options: Dashboard filters to the journal cursor

medium.prompt: A worker sent bytes but has not heard back. What should remove the job from pending delivery?

low.prompt: The dispatcher restarts after the receiver confirms success. What prevents replay?

light.mechanics: Changing the light changes the exposure available at a fixed aperture.
light.detail: Twice the light gives one stop more exposure at identical settings.

high.prompt: The rider moves from shade to bright sun while the camera settings stay fixed. What changed first?
options: The crop of the final image

medium.prompt: With fixed camera settings, doubling the light does what?

low.prompt: The scene light doubles at fixed settings. What changes?

frame.mechanics: Give a moving subject room in its direction of travel.
frame.detail: A crop alters composition, not the time recorded by the shutter.

high.prompt: The rider is too centered in the composition. Which change affects framing?
options: Move the rider toward the edge
Use a lower ISO at the same aperture and shutter time

medium.prompt: You crop the rider’s photo more tightly afterward. What happens to the exposure duration it recorded?
options: It follows the width of the crop

low.prompt: A client requests a digital crop around the rider. Which property actually changes?

exposure.mechanics: Use a shorter exposure to limit motion blur. Raise ISO to brighten the recorded result at the fixed aperture.
exposure.detail: This simplified scene is calibrated to 1/125 s at ISO 200. Moving from 1/125 to 1/500 loses two stops; ISO 800 offsets the brightness change, not the lost photons.

high.prompt: A moving rider smears while a parked bike stays sharp. What causes the smear?
options: The parked bike reflects less light
A wider crop in the viewfinder

medium.prompt: The rider is sharp but dark. At fixed aperture, how can you brighten the image and keep the shutter time?

low.prompt: In this scene, 1/125 s at ISO 200 becomes 1/500 s. Which ISO restores displayed brightness?

shutter.mechanics: A shorter exposure holds a moving subject closer to one position.
shutter.detail: Going from 1/125 to 1/500 shortens the recorded motion to one quarter at the same speed.

high.prompt: A moving rider looks blurred. Which camera control changes how long the motion is recorded?

medium.prompt: At fixed aperture, which setting gives the shortest motion trail for a rider at the same speed?

low.prompt: At fixed subject speed, going from 1/125 to 1/500 gives…
options: One quarter of the motion trail

iso.mechanics: Choose shutter speed for motion first, then compensate brightness when aperture is fixed.
iso.detail: Raising ISO cannot recover photons lost to a shorter exposure; noise may become more visible.

high.prompt: A sharp photo is too dark, and shutter time must stay fixed. Which adjustment can brighten it at fixed aperture?

medium.prompt: Higher ISO with the same shutter time will…
options: Reduce the time the shutter is open

low.prompt: Shutter time drops while aperture and scene light stay fixed. What can raising ISO do?
options: Restore the shorter motion trail to its previous length

pan.mechanics: Track the rider through the exposure so the background moves relative to the camera.
pan.detail: The closer subject and camera angular speeds match, the smaller the subject’s image displacement.

high.prompt: The photographer wants to pan as the rider passes. How should the camera move?
options: Point away from the rider during exposure
Follow the background past the rider

medium.prompt: Buildings streak behind a sharp rider in a panning shot. What did the camera follow?
options: The direction of the lane markings
Any subject moving at the same ground speed

low.prompt: How do you minimize displacement of the rider in frame?
options: Match only the distance to the road
